card.tagline: A pre-Inca Andean circle dance of Peru and Bolivia with fast flutes.
card.profile: The cachua is an indigenous Andean circle dance found in Peru, Bolivia, and Ecuador, with roots stretching back to the Inca period and earlier. Historically documented by Diego González Holguín in 1608, it is traditionally performed in rapid 2/4 time accompanied by flutes and drums. Today, it survives in regional celebrations such as the Carnaval Chico in Amantaní, Puno.
card.insight: In 1608, colonial lexicographer Diego González Holguín recorded the cachua as an ancient hand-holding Andean circle dance.

card.profile_long: The cachua, known variously as qachwa, qhaswa, kashua, kaswa, or kachura, is a traditional indigenous dance distributed across the central and southern Andes of Peru and Bolivia, with historical roots extending into Ecuador. As a pre-columbian indigenous tradition, its origins predate the Spanish conquest of Peru and were already practiced during the Inca period. In 1608, Diego González Holguín explicitly documented it in his lexicon as a dance where participants hold hands. During the late colonial period, the rhythm also crossed into baroque liturgical music, appearing in villancicos submitted in a report to Charles IV of Spain between 1788 and 1790. Musically, the cachua is characterized by rapid, unsyncopated two-four time where a quarter note alternates with two eighth notes across bars, accompanied by traditional pentatonic melodies. Traditional instrumentation relies heavily on indigenous flutes such as the quena and pan flutes, alongside drums, while string instruments like the charango or guitar may also be incorporated alongside paired vocal verses. Choreographically, it is executed as a circle dance involving pairs, distinguished by specific movements where men strike with their shoes and women spin around their own axis. Regional execution varies widely across the Andes. In contemporary practice, it manifests in specific localized forms such as the Qachwa de San Sebastián, a group Andean dance performed during the Carnaval Chico festival in the district of Amantaní, Puno. Whether found in historical baroque adaptations or modern Andean community celebrations, the cachua remains a vibrant connection to indigenous pre-Inca cultural expression.

sections.origins_and_history: The cachua dates back to the pre-Inca era and was practiced during the Inca period as a form of courtship. In 1608, Diego González Holguín noted it in his vocabulary of the general language of Peru as a hand-holding dance. Later, the style influenced colonial baroque music, appearing in Spanish-text villancicos with cachua rhythm sent to Charles IV of Spain around 1788 to 1790.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The cachua is performed as a circle dance involving pairs. Men strike the ground or rhythm with their shoes while women spin around their own axis. In Amantaní, Puno, it is executed as a group Andean dance during local festivities.
sections.music_and_instruments: It is played in a rapid, unsyncopated two-four time signature, featuring a pattern where a quarter note alternates with two eighth notes across bars. Melodies are traditionally pentatonic. Instrumentation includes native flutes like the quena and pan flutes, drums, and string instruments such as the charango or guitar, accompanied by singing with repeated verse pairs.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Occasions range from betrothals and Christmas celebrations to regional festivals like the Carnaval Chico de San Sebastián in Amantaní, Puno. Historically and in contemporary contexts, it serves as a community celebration and courting ritual.
sections.notable_figures: Diego González Holguín, who documented the dance in 1608.
sections.regional_variants: Found across the central and southern Andes of Peru, Bolivia, and Ecuador with differing local choreographies and instrumentations. Specific variants include the Qachwa de San Sebastián in Amantaní, Puno.
sections.lineage: Directly descended from pre-Inca indigenous traditions, maintained through the Inca period, adapted into colonial baroque villancicos, and preserved today as a living Andean folk and circle dance.
